items.article_search_text: Lando Norris has accepted the blame for colliding with Oscar Piastri in the Sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix on Saturday; watch every session of the United States GP in Austin on October 23-25, live on Sky Sports F1 Lando Norris says he let McLaren down and has taken responsibility for his collision with Oscar Piastri in the Sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix. Norris and Piastri made contact on the last lap of Saturday's shortened race when battling for fourth, which the stewards did not penalise either driver for. However, McLaren team principal Andrea Stella labelled the incident as "not acceptable" while Norris was not keen to talk about the collision on Saturday and told Sky Sports F1 : "As a team we all spoke about it. I apologised but that's all you need to know." Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 However, following his fourth-place finish in Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix, Norris changed his tune when speaking to the written media. "It's pretty straightforward. I can't attempt what I did. I should never have attempted in the first place, even if the move was on. I've got to think of the team that I represent more than myself," he said. "It was a mistake on my part, and I let down the team. I've also apologised to all of them, I owe them all an apology, and I will do better next time." Stella: Conversations with drivers not finished During Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix, Norris asked several times if he could aid team-mate Piastri in any way during the closing stages of the race. Piastri was attempting to catch and overtake Lewis Hamilton at the time of the radio calls, suggesting Norris was querying whether he should back up the Ferrari driver. In the end, Piastri overtook Hamilton without any help to finish fifth behind Norris. Stella says he was "very encouraged" by Norris' willingness to aid his team-mate but more talks will be held before the United States Grand Prix in Austin next weekend. "We are aligned as to how we want to lead this team forward in a joint effort between the team and the drivers," he said. "The conversations that we are having, they are not finished but it's not because we need to go back discussing if Lando was alongside Oscar, that's not the interesting bit. "For me the interesting bit is a reflection that all the stakeholders, the team, the drivers will have to make around leading together the team, embracing constantly from inside the cockpit the interest of the team, as something that is superior to any particular singular individual interest. "While the conversations from this point of view, they are not concluded and there's more we can do to become a more united and even stronger team, I'm pleased that Lando at some stage in the race adopted this way of thinking. "This is what I expect as a team principal, this is what the 1000 people that work at McLaren expect from our drivers so it's good that we read this example. I expect definitely more of that in the future, independently of the fact that they will be heard in the radio, or they will happen behind the closed door in every meeting or in the way we approach our race plan." items.article_search_text: Sky Sports F1s Martin Brundle gives his verdict on Max Verstappens dominant weekend in Singapore, Lewis Hamiltons decision to not pit under a Virtual Safety Car and the Sprint collision between McLarens Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri It was a full-on weekend of F1, with a Sprint race added to the street circuit schedule. Coming at the end of a demanding run of six Grands Prix in seven weeks, it was a significant challenge for everyone involved, not just the teams and drivers. I've always enjoyed the Singapore Grand Prix, right from the first race, despite the relentless heat and humidity that can leave you feeling like you need a shower barely five minutes into the day. The city is buzzing, the event has a fantastic atmosphere and the F1 cars are relentlessly pounding around the circuit. With just one practice session followed by two qualifying sessions and two races, it makes for an action-packed weekend. However, what took the shine off things a little this year was the unusually poor air quality caused by crop burning in neighbouring countries. Singapore has long held the mantle as F1's 'business' Grand Prix, combining world-class motorsport with a top-tier music festival. A record combined crowd of more than 300,000 underlined its appeal, making it an event well worth adding to your bucket list if you haven't already been. How Kimi Antonelli could win F1 world title as soon as the next race F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column Download the Sky Sports app for expert analysis, best video & more 📱 Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 Russell's Sprint crash sums up his season It was very much Max Verstappen and Red Bull's weekend, with the Dutchman winning both the Sprint and the Grand Prix from pole position. Combined with his victory at Sepang in Malaysia a few days earlier, that made it three wins in a row. Verstappen is still too far behind to mount another 'Chucky' championship comeback like last season, but he has climbed to fourth in the standings, just eight points behind Lewis Hamilton and 17 behind second-placed George Russell. However, he remains 119 points adrift of championship leader Kimi Antonelli, with 150 points still available, assuming all the remaining races go ahead amid ongoing global conflicts. After a surprise storm delay and a couple of laps behind the Safety Car, the Sprint finally got under way. George made an impressive start to take the lead from second on the grid, but carried too much speed and throttle into the pit straight at the end of the opening lap, spinning into the concrete barriers. With major power unit penalties already looming for the Grand Prix, this was his best opportunity to make an impact. The images of him sliding across the white line and wet kerbs felt like a fitting summary of his season so far. This left Max out in front, with Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari keeping him honest, while Charles Leclerc began to drop back in the second Ferrari as he struggled more than most with his worn intermediate tyres. Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris kept a close watch in their McLarens, which had shown strong pace throughout the weekend. Both were closing in on Leclerc, with Antonelli's Mercedes also being drawn into the battle. However, with the track still damp and the kerbs slippery, there was little incentive to take unnecessary risks with the main qualifying session and Grand Prix still to come. The priority was to bring the cars home safely and collect whatever Sprint points were on offer, before attention turned to the bigger prizes ahead. Norris' overtake attempt on Piastri a lunge too far Lando had other ideas. He had looked a little quicker than Oscar throughout, although not quite enough to overtake easily. Heading into Turn 5 on the final lap, having seemingly been sizing up the move for several laps, Norris sliced down Oscar's right-hand side to claim the corner and position. The pair touched and spun in a synchronised pirouette, with Piastri's car hitting the wall. McLaren are in a battle now with Red Bull for third in the championship when not so long ago they were catching Ferrari in a battle for second. These positions mean huge amounts prize money for 2027, along with the kudos and season long pitlane position, and likely partner/sponsor bonuses. Money and resource spent on 2026 parts can also impact on the 2027 car now. The team didn't care which driver was in front, they just wanted them home undamaged in fourth and fifth. The only consolation was Lando recovered for a point in eighth. Drivers are hard wired to simply race, and think of their own goals, that's why they do what they do, but whilst there was a gap against his team-mate, who could perhaps have given more space assuming he even saw it coming, it was a risky move and a lunge too far from Lando. We understand McLaren team bosses were extremely unhappy with that one. Through all the chaos Antonelli steered nicely around everything to claim a fortunate third from seventh on the Sprint grid yet again extending his championship lead. His patience continues to pay off. Verstappen had all bases covered Having never taken pole position in Singapore before, Max Verstappen followed up his Sprint success by securing pole for the main race. The data suggested that either Ferrari could have claimed pole had they extracted the full potential from their laps. Regardless, Charles Leclerc came close to beating Verstappen to the first corner, but the Red Bull driver had the advantage of a fresh set of soft tyres and used them to squeeze Leclerc into submission. The field settled into race order relatively quickly. Starting from the back, George Russell could only climb to 17th in the opening stages, such was the intensity and competitiveness of the midfield. Isack Hadjar, starting from the pitlane in the similarly displaced Red Bull, faced an even tougher challenge. This is a good opportunity to give Liam Lawson a deserved shout-out. Driving for Racing Bulls, he finished seventh in the challenging conditions at Sepang the previous week, followed that up with fifth in the Singapore Sprint and then secured another seventh-place finish in Sunday's Grand Prix. As the highest-placed driver outside the top four teams, Lawson put together an excellent run across a demanding series of races. Out front, Verstappen had the Grand Prix firmly under control. Although Leclerc kept him honest in the opening stages, the Dutchman was eventually able to build a comfortable gap, giving Red Bull greater flexibility with its strategy and the freedom to react calmly to the tactics of its rivals or the potential intervention of a Safety Car. Impossible to run a modern F1 car and team from behind the wheel Hamilton started on a fresh set of medium tyres but began to struggle as the race progressed. Appearing to be on a clear two-stop strategy, he pitted as early as lap 18 for soft tyres. Bizarrely, he would not stop again, despite the opportunity to make a relatively cheap pit stop under a Virtual Safety Car (VSC) when Lance Stroll's stricken Aston Martin had to be cleared from the circuit. Hamilton then endured a relentless slide down the order, eventually losing fifth place to Oscar Piastri's McLaren in the closing stages, despite the Australian having made an unscheduled stop for a slow puncture. After the race, it emerged that switching to a one-stop strategy, which required him to complete 44 laps on the same tyres, had been Hamilton's own decision. He apologised to the team for the call. It is difficult to run a modern F1 car and manage the team's strategy from behind the wheel, and the incident was telling. Ferrari had seemingly expected Hamilton to pit under the VSC. Lando Norris had been pressuring the struggling Hamilton before making a late move down the inside into Turn 1. Both drivers ran wide, Hamilton more so, and as they scrambled back onto the circuit with dirty tyres, championship leader Kimi Antonelli seized his opportunity to sweep past them both. The move secured him third place, ahead of his two closest title rivals, and extended his championship lead once again. It was an impressive display of maturity, particularly given that Mercedes no longer appears to have the fastest car on the grid. Norris and Piastri secured a solid fourth and fifth for McLaren, while a tenacious drive from Nico Hulkenberg in his Audi limited George Russell to just two points in ninth. Isack Hadjar claimed the final point in 10th after starting from the pitlane in his Red Bull, capping an impressive recovery drive. It was hardly a classic Grand Prix, in Singapore or anywhere else, but there was no shortage of stories and drama amid the stifling humidity. Next stop: Austin, Texas. Oscar Piastri has battled to a hard-fought fifth place at the Singapore Grand Prix, helping his McLaren team salvage some pride and useful championship points from an otherwise frustrating weekend at the Marina Bay Street Circuit. Australian star Piastri finished one place behind team-mate Lando Norris, just outside the podium spots, but the day after both McLaren drivers received a public dressing down from team chiefs for a collision between them on the final lap of Saturday’s Sprint race, the Grand Prix result can be judged a positive outcome. The weekend, however, really belonged to Red Bull flyer Max Verstappen, who roared home to victory on his 250th Grand Prix start, capping a remarkable 24 hours in which the four-time world champ also banked two pole positions and a classy victory in the Sprint race. Starting from his 50th career pole place, it was the Dutchman’s second straight victory after winning the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia last weekend, and leaves him fourth in the championship standings. Verstappen’s triumph means Red Bull are now seven points behind constructors’ champions McLaren in the battle for third place. “It’s taken a while but I think this race was very good. We had pace when we needed to have it on the soft tyre, even though I think the medium tyre for everyone was more of a struggle,” Verstappen said. “But it worked out, so of course very happy to win here... The last two races have been really positive for us and it’s just great to see.” Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc finished second while Mercedes driver Kimi Antonelli was third, extending his championship lead over teammate George Russell to 102 points and knowing he can mathematically win his maiden title in the next round in Austin, Texas from 23-25 October. “Can I? Really?”, 20-year-old Italian Antonelli said when he was told after his 14th podium of the season. “Well, let’s not worry about that. items.article_search_text: Lando Norris and his McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri crashed on the final lap of the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint; the incident cost McLaren eight championship points; watch Sundays Singapore Grand Prix at 1pm (build-up from 11.30am) live on Sky Sports F1 Lando Norris has revealed he was "told off" by McLaren following a collision with team-mate Oscar Piastri during the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint that team principal Andrea Stella said was "not acceptable". Norris had narrowly trailed Piastri in a battle for fourth for most of the 20-lap race at the Marina Bay Street Circuit, where overtaking is extremely difficult. Norris tried to go up the inside of Turn 5 on the final circuit, which led to a crash as Piastri turned in, with the Australian spun around as his rear-right tyre was struck by his team-mate's front-left. Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺 Piastri suffered damage that took him out of the race, while Norris was able to get going again and take the chequered flag in eighth for the final point. After summoning the drivers for a hearing, the stewards decided not to take any action as they deemed that both had contributed to the collision. However, the general consensus in the paddock was that Norris, who had been trailing and attempted the pass, was more responsible. Norris initially insisted he believed the pass had been on, but speaking later on Saturday following qualifying and discussions with Piastri and the McLaren hierarchy, he told Sky Sports F1 : "As a team we all spoke about it. I apologised but that's all you need to know." Pushed by Sky Italy for details of the discussions, he added: "I was told off." Piastri retained a calm outlook on the incident, but said: "It was clear those kind of things can't happen. Everyone knows where we sit. "We will all be fine and keep pushing together like we always do." Stella: Incident simply not acceptable McLaren team principal Andrea Stella said the incident was "not acceptable" but chose not to single out either of his drivers for criticism. "It's been a long day," Stella told Sky Sports F1 . "The Sprint race was a race that was giving us some good points, in a moment in which we are not in condition to win. Still, we were in condition to score good points. "And we saw two McLarens having contact, basically going out of the race. Lando could score one point but definitely that's not enough. "Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable. "This is something that we will discuss with our drivers. We will do it in private. We will reiterate that the team interest is far bigger than any of us. There's no ego, there's no person that's bigger than the interest of the McLaren F1 team. This will be reiterated. "I'm sure, like always, there will be conversations that will lead to the team being more united and even stronger." Brundle: Not smart from Norris The move Norris attempted was "not smart", according to Sky Sports F1's Martin Brundle. Speaking on commentary immediately after the incident, Brundle said: "McLaren will be furious about that, on the final lap of a Sprint. "Whether they were fourth or fifth, it would have made no difference to the team whatsoever." The difference between finishing fourth and fifth in a Sprint is only one point. McLaren were on course to collect nine points, but instead ended up taking just one and seeing their lead over Red Bull in the battle for third in the constructors' standings cut to just 11 points. Brundle suggested that reigning world champion Norris was largely responsible for the collision. "That was not smart, Lando. That was not smart at all," Brundle said. "I think Lando got on the kerb on the inside as the space pinched a little bit and that slid him even more into the side of his team-mate. "It just wasn't worth the risk. What was Oscar going to do? I know they're racers. It just wasn't worth taking the risk just to swap the two cars around in a Sprint." Norris insists pass was on Norris immediately apologised to his team over the radio but insisted in his post-session interview that he thought the move was on. The Brit said over team radio: "Sorry about that. Obviously I didn't want that to happen but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space at the apex but I was there, so..." Quizzed over the incident in his post-race interview with Sky Sports F1 , Norris added: "I'd rather just go back and review it." On whether he still believed "the move was on", Norris said: "It was." Piastri played down the incident, claiming he wasn't "that bothered" due to the fact it was a Sprint event. "I've not seen it properly," the Australian told Sky Sports F1 . "From where I sit, I'm not...it's for fourth and fifth for a Sprint race so I'm not that bothered either way. Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed. "Just a shame for the team." 'A hell of a lunge' Sky Sports F1 pundit and former world champion Jenson Button described Norris' move as "a hell of a lunge". Reflecting on Norris' comments after the incident, Button said: "He was very bullish. Normally when you're that bullish, you're being defensive. "It was a hell of a lunge. On your team-mate, at that moment in a race. "And the problem is the corner does tighten quite a lot at the apex and he found himself in the side of his team-mate." Max Verstappen won the sprint race and followed up by securing pole position at the F1 Singapore Grand Prix, but Australia's Oscar Piastri had to settle for seventh spot after an earlier collision with teammate Lando Norris in the sprint. Verstappen qualified first on the grid by 0.054 of a second ahead of Ferrari's Charles Leclerc, with British veteran Lewis Hamilton third and F1 Championship leader Kimi Antonelli fourth. Besides Verstappen, the day's other big winner was Antonelli, who widened his lead over George Russell when his Mercedes teammate crashed out from the lead in the sprint. Piastri's McLaren teammate Lando Norris was fifth but they will be next to each other on row three in Sunday's Grand Prix because of a penalty for Briton Russell. The two collided in the last lap of the sprint race fighting for fourth place, with Norris limping home in eighth and Piastri not finishing. World champion Norris apologised ‌to his McLaren team after the knock which saw him attempt an overtake but clipped the Australian's rear tyre sending both cars spinning and handing Antonelli fourth place. "Sorry about that. Obviously I didn't want that to happen but I thought I was fully alongside. I just ran out of space ‌at the apex but ‌I was there," ⁠Norris said over the team radio. While Norris limped home to eighth place to claim the ​final point available, Piastri was forced to retire as he became one of nine cars that did not finish - a record number of retirements for a Formula One sprint race. Piastri said he had not seen the incident but downplayed its significance as they were not in ‌high points ​scoring positions. "From where I sit, it's for fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so I'm not that bothered either way," Piastri ​said. "Just obviously it's ‌a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed (ahead of qualifying for Sunday's race). Just a shame ​for the team." Both McLaren drivers were summoned to meet the stewards after the collision but no further action was taken. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella was not impressed with ​his drivers, however, adding that scoring just one point was not ‌enough. "Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable. This is something that we will discuss with our drivers," he said. "We will do it in private. We will reiterate that the team interest is far bigger than any of us. There's no ego, there's no person that is bigger than the interest of the McLaren Formula One team." Russell beat Verstappen off the line at the start in wet conditions but lost control when he put a wheel on a painted line at the end of the first lap, spinning across the track and into the barrier. Antonelli was fourth, extending his lead over Russell from 84 points to 89, after he picked up two positions on the last lap when Norris and Piastri collided ahead of him. items.article_search_text: Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri's collision at the end of the Singapore sprint race went unpunished by Formula 1's stewards, who declared "both drivers had contributed to the incident." Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri’s collision at the end of the Singapore sprint race went unpunished by Formula 1’s stewards, who declared “both drivers had contributed to the incident.” Norris tried a late and optimistic pass on his McLaren teammate down the inside of Turn 5 on the final lap, but collided as Piastri moved across to take the corner himself. The McLaren drivers had been running fourth and fifth when the incident occurred. McLaren’s rules of on-track engagement was one of the biggest Formula 1 storylines of the past two years -- infamously dubbed ‘Papaya Rules’ by team boss Andrea Stella in 2024, a nod to the papaya shade of orange on the team’s cars. Saturday’s collision took Piastri out of the race completely, although Norris recovered to finish eighth, collecting a single point in the process. Norris seemed irritated when asked about the move afterwards by Viaplay. Asked if it was unnecessary, he replied: “What, to go for a big gap? Or overtake?” He then asked the journalist: “What’s the title of the race? Sprint ... What’s after sprint?” When the journalist replied “race,” Norris replied: “Wow, good job. Yeah, it’s race!” The stewards deemed neither driver was predominantly to blame. In a verdict released just as qualifying for Sunday’s grand prix started, the stewards said both could have avoided the incident which occurred. The statement read: “The driver of Car 81 explained that he had not expected Car 1 to attempt an overtake and, after turning in, noticed Car 1 on the inside and attempted to leave space. The driver of Car 1 said that he saw an opportunity to overtake. He said that the front axle of his car was ahead of the mirror of Car 81 prior to the apex and therefore expected to be left space. “As he approached the apex, the space was less than he had anticipated so he had to use the inside kerb and braked and a collision occurred. The Stewards considered that both drivers had contributed to the incident and that neither driver was wholly or predominantly to blame for the collision. Therefore the Stewards determined to take no further action.”

Norris escapes a penalty after the Singapore Sprint clash. Piastri’s race ends at Turn 5. The stewards blame neither McLaren driver outright. Lando Norris has escaped punishment after his final-lap collision with Oscar Piastri in the Singapore Grand Prix Sprint, with the F1 stewards ruling that both drivers contributed to the crash. The verdict closes a tense crash investigation into a move that ended one car’s race and spun the other away from a likely points haul. Piastri was running fourth when Norris launched an inside attack at Turn 5. Their McLarens made contact at the apex, sending both off track; Piastri hit the barrier and retired, while Norris recovered to finish eighth and score one point. For McLaren, the incident transformed a potential fourth-and-fifth finish worth nine points into a single point. The stewards’ verdict: no penalty decision and no further action. Singapore Sprint crash investigation: what happened at Turn 5 Norris saw a passing opportunity on the final lap and committed to the inside line. He told the stewards that his front axle had moved ahead of Piastri’s mirror before the apex, leading him to expect room on the inside. As the gap narrowed, Norris used the kerb and braked, but his left-front tyre clipped Piastri’s right-rear. Piastri said he did not expect his team-mate to attack there. After turning into the corner, he spotted the orange car and tried to leave space, but the contact sent both cars into a spin. The Australian struck the barrier and retired on the spot; Norris rejoined and brought his damaged car home in eighth. The sequence was abrupt, but the stewards’ account points to a shared misjudgement rather than a one-sided hit. https://www.youtube.com/watch?vJhdzK3uO7qg F1 stewards explain the penalty decision The stewards reviewed video and in-car footage, then heard from both drivers and team representatives. Their finding was that Norris attempted the overtake and misjudged how much room remained, while Piastri also contributed as he turned into the corner. Neither driver, the report concluded, carried sole or predominant responsibility. That distinction explains why the stewards’ verdict stopped short of a penalty. A collision does not automatically trigger a sanction; the officials weighed the positioning, the available space and each driver’s account. The outcome differs from other close calls, such as the Leclerc-Piastri collision debate, where the circumstances and driver assessments shaped the story. Here, the ruling leaves both McLaren racers without an official penalty. What the Singapore verdict means for McLaren The result carries a blunt sporting cost: McLaren lost eight points against the nine-point return its cars appeared set to secure, while Norris salvaged one. The official ruling protects both drivers from a penalty, but it does not erase the damage to the team’s Sprint tally or the lost chance to convert a strong position into a double points finish. For Norris and Piastri, the immediate work is internal: review the onboard footage, agree how they judge space in a late-race fight, and avoid turning a shared error into a wider team fault line. The stewards’ call settles the formal case; McLaren still has to manage the sporting fallout. items.article_search_text: There was more disappointment for Australian driver Oscar Piastri as Max Verstappen claimed the rain-marred Singapore Grand Prix... Max Verstappen won the Singapore Grand Prix sprint race after George Russell crashed out from the lead, missing a chance to cut his Mercedes teammate Kimi Antonelli's advantage in the hunt for the Formula One title. In a chaotic race on Saturday that also saw Lando Norris collide with his McLaren teammate, Australia's Oscar Piastri, Russell beat Verstappen off the line at the start in wet conditions but lost control when he put a wheel on a painted line at the end of the first lap, spinning across the track and into the barrier. The British driver tapped his hands against the car in frustration as he climbed out. "I'm fine. Sorry, sorry, sorry," he told Mercedes over the radio. Verstappen eased to the win after that, backing up his victory in Malaysia last week, with Ferrari duo Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc second and third. Antonelli was fourth, extending his lead over Russell from 84 points to 89, after he picked up two positions on the last lap when Norris and Piastri collided ahead of him. Norris tried an ambitious overtake down the inside of his teammate but badly misjudged it and sent the Australian spinning into the barrier. McLaren chief executive Zak Brown shook his head in dismay on the pit wall. Russell has a grid penalty for Sunday's Grand Prix, meaning the 20-year-old Antonelli could take another big step towards becoming F1's youngest-ever champion. Russell wasn't the only driver to be caught out in the wet conditions. He was one of eight non-finishers after a spate of collisions and technical problems, with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar stopped by car trouble. Verstappen said Red Bull will need to work on its "horrendous" starts after he lost the lead off the line, just as he did in Malaysia last week. "We don't accelerate off the line," he said. "Up until now we always have terrible starts, so we need to understand what's going on there." New Zealander Liam Lawson was fifth for Racing Bulls, with Haas's Oliver Bearman sixth and Nico Hulkenberg seventh for Audi. Norris recovered to claim a point in eighth in the last sprint of 2026. The start was delayed because of heavy rain, making it the second week running that an F1 race has started late. Last week's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia was first held up by a downpour, then because several cars' software failed to cope with the wet conditions. The FIA issued a software update that was also being used in Singapore this week. Qualifying is later on Saturday for the Singapore Grand Prix on Sunday. Australian Associated Press

items.article_search_text: Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri collided in the sprint race at the Singapore GP, yet the reigning champion insists the move was on After lengthy delays before the F1 sprint race at the Singapore Grand Prix, McLaren were on for a decent finish at the Marina Bay Circuit. However, on the final lap of the race, Lando Norris collided with his teammate, Oscar Piastri , at Turn 5, whilst the duo were running in fourth and fifth, with Piastri in the lead car. After the incident, Norris was able to get going again and crossed the line in eighth place, securing one point for the team. The British driver is now under investigation by the FIA and will have to report to the stewards before qualifying. But on the other side of the garage, Piastri was not able to finish the sprint race and was one of the nine drivers who failed to finish the 20-lap sprint. Immediately after the race, the reigning F1 world champion was asked about his point of view on the collision. “I'd rather just go back and review it,” Norris told Sky Sports. When asked if the move was on, Norris said, “It was… I apologize to them that one of the cars is out, but like I said, the rest of it we'll go review." On the other side of the incident, Piastri, who was leading his teammate, ended up with nothing to show from the sprint race. The Australian driver had not seen the incident again when he spoke to the media, and was more interested in the amount of work that the team would have to do before the Grand Prix qualifying session. “I've not seen it properly. I mean, from where I sit, it's fourth and fifth for a sprint race, so not that bothered either way,” Piastri admitted. “Just obviously it's a lot of work now for the team to get both cars fixed, so, just a shame for the team.” Due to the delays caused by the weather conditions ahead of the sprint race, there are further delays to the qualifying session later in the day. These delays will give McLaren time to get Norris and Piastri’s cars ready for the chance to get decent grid slots for the Grand Prix on Sunday. Stay up to date with all of the breaking sport, politics, entertainment, finance, weather and business headlines. Today's news, live updates & all the latest breaking stories from 7NEWS. Max Verstappen has lit up the streets of Singapore to pip George Russell to sprint pole while Australian hope Oscar Piastri forced his way into fourth place. The action was overshadowed when the cars’ settings were wrongly changed by race control, affecting the cars and blamed for some drivers being eliminated from the session early. Verstappen who claimed his first win of the F1 season at the Bahrain Grand Prix held in Malaysia last weekend, was in imperious form again as his Red Bull showed further signs of progress. “It is always close in Singapore, your lap — you are pushing as close as you can to the walls. I did not expect this, very happy to be first,” Verstappen said. Russell saved his best until last but was unable to topple the four-time world champion, finishing 0.120 seconds adrift as he bumped Ferrari’s Charles Leclerc down to third. Piastri claimed fourth for Saturday’s 21-lap dash, ahead of McLaren teammate Lando Norris and Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton. Runaway championship leader Kimi Antonelli was off the pace throughout the session and could manage only seventh – 0.693sec off the pace to raise further doubts over the upgrade Mercedes brought last weekend. Antonelli has one hand on the title after team-mate Russell’s power-unit failure in the closing stages last week gave the Italian an 84-point lead with just seven rounds to run. Russell, running the Mercedes car without the upgrade, will start the main race on Sunday from the back of the grid after taking a new power unit, in a further blow to his slender title hopes. Verstappen was summoned by the stewards in an investigation into whether he overtook Lewis Hamilton earlier in the qualifying session under yellow flags, but he was not penalised. Cars were down on power for several minutes in the first part of Friday’s qualifying session because “overtake mode” — an electrical power boost activated by the drivers — was disabled. Williams team principal James Vowles said the issue played a role in both of his drivers being eliminated, with Alex Albon 19th and Carlos Sainz, Jr. 22nd. The FIA blamed “a human error in race control” which meant cars were blocked from using overtake mode after the session was briefly red-flagged. The setting was then switched back on for 27 seconds, and switched off again. “The FIA acknowledges that this unfortunate human error had an impact on the performance of certain cars based on the timing of their run and their position around the lap,” the governing body said. It’s the latest in a series of issues with the software which governs the 2026 cars’ electrical power and comes five days after cars crawled to a halt in the rain in Malaysia, delaying the race start. Leclerc led Hamilton in a Ferrari one-two in a second session delayed by 16 minutes after Verstappen had topped the first, to hint at an open fight for pole. So it proved but it was Verstappen who pulled the stellar lap out the bag in the closing stages and the four-time world champion will hope to continue his step forward with sprint victory on Saturday. According to the McLaren driver, Red Bull’s progress may not have received enough attention because Verstappen did not start from the front in Baku and also faced an engine problem.Piastri feels Verstappen could have challenged Mercedes driver George Russell much earlier in that race if he had started higher up the grid.He said, “I think whatever Red Bull put on their car in Baku clearly was big, because I think Baku kind of went under the radar for them, with where they qualified and Max's engine problem. I think if he had started at the front in Baku, I think it would've...he put George under a lot of pressure at the end of the race, but I think he would've put George under a lot of pressure for the whole race. And then, obviously, in Malaysia, he was definitely the quickest car and driver combination.”Mercedes no longer alone at the top?Oscar Piastri also feels the gap between the leading teams is becoming smaller. Us and Ferrari kind of seem to and fro a little bit, but Mercedes have always been the class of the field.
